introduction: This small guide collects what the writings say about spelling, grammar and the letters of the alphabet. Some of it is practical: how the Greatest Name is to be written, why copies of a Tablet differ, the plan for a universal language. Some is the Báb’s symbolic science of letters. And some is defence: the Báb’s Arabic broke the grammarians’ rules, His critics said so, and Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answered that the revealer of a language is not bound by its schoolmasters. The same charge and answer are in the New Testament, “how knoweth this man letters, having never learned?” and Paul’s “rude in speech, yet not in knowledge”. Confucius on correct names, the shibboleth, Babel and Pentecost, the Qur’an’s mysterious letters and its “Lecture in Arabic” are other moments when letters and language carry religious weight.
questions: Why should a revelation be free of the grammar of its language? Why might critics think the question matters?
Reading 1 admits that copies differ. Does a scripture need to be textually perfect to be authoritative?
What is lost in translation, according to Ben Sira’s grandson, and how do the readings propose to live with it?
Why do so many traditions find meaning in single letters?

outside.why: Many Tablets went out without being checked, hence disparities between copies. The Psalmist’s ideal of scripture: the words of the Lord are pure words, as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. How does a reader hold that ideal together with the reading’s frank account of copying?
Good writing is the ordered presentation of signs. Confucius: if names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things.
How the Greatest Name is to be spelled and said. Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right.
“Light” and “radiance” mean the same in language, yet differ. There are so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without signification.
In Arabic “man” and “human” do not differ. Ben Sira’s grandson, translating: the same things uttered in Hebrew, and translated into another tongue, have not the same force in them.
Hundreds of names for the camel; each nation’s tongue and a universal one. And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.
A letter that “contains much meaning”. The Qur’an’s second chapter opens with three letters and no explanation: Alif. Lám. Mím.
The creation of grammar “from around the mystery of the line”. In the beginning was the Word.
When letters enter their gardens all languages become one. They began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending: God named by two letters.
“In my youth I paid no heed to the schools’ canons.” How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?

The Báb abrogated the rules of language and freed the Arabic tongue. The Qur’an’s own claim was clarity in the language as it stood: We have revealed it, a Lecture in Arabic, that ye may understand. What is gained, and what is risked, when a scripture breaks the grammar of its language?
Charges of grammatical error come from ignorance, as with the Arabs of old. Paul: though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge.

The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life. Critics of the Báb’s Arabic and defenders alike appeal to something beyond grammar. Is “the spirit, not the letter” a fair answer to a charge of solecism?

shortfall: Readings 4, 8, 9, 12 and 14 are points of spelling, verb forms and script on which nothing outside bears.
